aka: TFClass: more than 3 adjacent zinc finger factors
short: CTCF is a single, near-ubiquitously expressed protein whose eleven C2H2 zinc fingers read an asymmetric, roughly 15-20 bp GC-rich sequence, often with a second recognition module a few bases upstream. Tens of thousands of these sites act as insulators and as anchors for cohesin-extruded chromatin loops, so they delimit topologically associating domains and separate enhancers from promoters they should not reach. Because the motif is long, information-rich, and read by a well-characterized finger-to-base code solved in two crystal structures, a CTCF match is one of the few motif hits that predicts real occupancy reasonably often. The site is directional: which strand it lies on determines which way a loop is anchored, and convergent pairs of sites are the ones that form loops.
long:
## The factors

CTCF (CCCTC-binding factor) is one protein, not a family. The human gene encodes a 727-residue polypeptide with a central array of eleven Cys2-His2 zinc fingers flanked by N- and C-terminal regions that carry no DNA-binding domain. It is expressed in essentially every cell type examined, and it is extraordinarily conserved: the chicken and human proteins are 93% identical in amino acid sequence (Filippova et al. 1996) [PMID:8649389]. CTCF binds DNA as a monomer; no dimerization interface is required, and its long-range activity comes from partners rather than from self-assembly. The most important of these is cohesin: a short segment in the CTCF N terminus docks onto the SA2-SCC1 (STAG2-RAD21) surface of human cohesin, and a 2.7 A crystal structure of that complex showed the interaction is specifically needed for CTCF-anchored loops and for positioning cohesin at CTCF sites (Li et al. 2020) [PMID:31905366]. CTCF has exactly one paralogue, the testis-restricted CTCFL/BORIS, which carries an almost identical zinc-finger array and is treated as a separate family here.

## The motif

The high-information core is 15 bp. JASPAR's core model (MA0139.2) reduces to RCCASYAGRKGGCRS in IUPAC, which is the sequence most people mean when they write the CTCF consensus; longer ChIP-derived models are also in use (JASPAR MA1929.2 and MA1930.2 span 31 and 33 positions), corresponding to the 33/34-mer that Schmidt et al. (2012) defined from six mammals [PMID:22244452]. The structural basis is unusually well understood. In the Hashimoto et al. (2017) crystal structure, zinc fingers 3-7 each contact three bases of the 15-bp core, with each conserved nucleotide making a base-specific hydrogen bond to a particular side chain; variable positions also make contacts, which is how CTCF tolerates deviation from consensus [PMID:28529057]. Yin et al. (2017) resolved CTCF on protocadherin sites and split the site into four modules: ZF3 reads module 4, ZF4-7 read modules 3 and 2, and ZF9-11 read an upstream module 1, with ZF8 acting as a spacer that absorbs variable distance between modules 1 and 2 [PMID:29076501]. Genome-wide, ZF4-7 anchor CTCF at roughly 80% of targets containing the core motif, while ZF1-2 and ZF8-11 read non-conserved flanks (Nakahashi et al. 2013) [PMID:23707059]. Two consequences matter in practice. The site is asymmetric, so it has an orientation, and a central asymmetric A is part of what makes recognition directional [PMID:29076501]. CTCF is also sensitive to cytosine methylation at position 2 of the core but insensitive at position 12, a difference the structure rationalizes [PMID:28529057]; across 19 human cell types, 41% of variable CTCF occupancy was attributable to differential methylation concentrated at two positions in the recognition sequence (Wang et al. 2012) [PMID:22955980].

## Where it acts

The first genome-wide survey reported 13,804 CTCF sites (Kim et al. 2007) [PMID:17382889]; current ChIP-seq gives tens of thousands per cell type. Sites are GC-rich but are not concentrated in CpG islands the way GC-box promoters are; they are spread across intergenic space, introns and promoter-proximal regions, and lineage-specific expansions have been driven by waves of retrotransposon activity (Schmidt et al. 2012) [PMID:22244452]. Occupied sites are enriched at topologically associating domain boundaries, where they often occur in clusters rather than singly, a redundancy that appears to stabilize boundaries over evolution (Kentepozidou et al. 2020) [PMID:31910870]. The essential partner is cohesin. Loops form preferentially between CTCF sites in convergent orientation (Rao et al. 2014) [PMID:25497547], and deleting or inverting a single site changes the loops formed (de Wit et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2015) [PMID:26527277,26276636] - the observation that motivated the loop-extrusion model (Sanborn et al. 2015; Fudenberg et al. 2016) [PMID:26499245,27210764] and that single-molecule work later explained as DNA-tension-dependent, orientation-specific blocking of extruding cohesin (Davidson et al. 2023) [PMID:37076620].

## Biology and disease

CTCF was defined functionally as the protein required for enhancer-blocking by vertebrate insulators (Bell et al. 1999) [PMID:10458613] and for methylation-sensitive imprinting control at the H19/Igf2 locus [PMID:10839546,10839547]. Acute degradation of CTCF abolishes CTCF-CTCF loops and TAD insulation while leaving A/B compartments intact, separating those two layers of genome folding (Nora et al. 2017) [PMID:28525758]. In disease, CTCF/cohesin-binding sites are recurrent somatic mutation hotspots in several cancers (Katainen et al. 2015) [PMID:26053496]; in IDH-mutant glioma, hypermethylation disrupts a CTCF boundary and allows an enhancer to activate PDGFRA (Flavahan et al. 2016) [PMID:26700815]; and germline monoallelic CTCF variants cause an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder affecting brain, growth and craniofacial development (Valverde de Morales et al. 2023) [PMID:36454652].

## Reading a hit

This is the one family in the atlas where a position-weight-matrix match genuinely carries predictive weight: sites that match the consensus more closely are occupied more often and more constitutively (Plasschaert et al. 2014) [PMID:24121688]. Even so, only a fraction of genomic matches are bound in any one cell type, and occupancy is conditional on the methylation state of the CpG at core position 2. Report the strand: a CTCF hit without an orientation is half an answer, because loop anchoring depends on it. A hit cannot distinguish CTCF from CTCFL, which share the zinc-finger array. Finally, check which matrix matched. Two Vierstra archetypes labelled for CTCF are not the CTCF motif at all - AC0214:CTCF/ZNF is a poly-T model (tTTTTgTTTTT) and AC0174:CTCF/ZNF is a short C-rich model (tGCCCCCT, 8.4 bits) - and a hit to either says nothing about CTCF. The genuine CTCF models, including the ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO core model (CTCF.H14CORE.0.P.B, ChIP evidence, grade B), agree with each other and with two independent crystal structures [PMID:28529057,29076501], so the label itself is not in doubt.
caveats: Trust a strong CTCF hit more than almost any other motif in this atlas, but not unconditionally. Only some matches are occupied in a given cell type; occupancy depends on the methylation state of the CpG at core position 2, and a site bound in one lineage may be free in another. The hit cannot tell CTCF from CTCFL/BORIS. Orientation is part of the result, not an afterthought. A single site is weak evidence for a domain boundary, since boundaries are usually clusters of sites. And confirm which matrix matched: two Vierstra archetypes carrying the CTCF label are poly-T or short C-rich models that have nothing to do with the CTCF core.

timeline.finding: A 5' element of the chicken beta-globin domain (the HS4 region) is shown to block the beta-globin LCR enhancer from a reporter directionally, and to protect a transgene from position effects in Drosophila, establishing the vertebrate insulator as an element that can be assayed.
timeline.methods: Stable reporter assays in K562 erythroid cells; transgenic Drosophila position-effect assay
timeline.open: No protein had been identified that bound the element or carried its activity.

timeline.finding: Cloning of human CTCF shows an 11-zinc-finger protein 93% identical between chicken and human that binds diverged c-myc promoter sites with different subsets of fingers (ZF2-7 on the chicken site, ZF3-11 on the human), the first evidence that CTCF is 'multivalent'.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, gel shifts with finger deletions, contact-base mutagenesis, proteolytic protection
timeline.open: Because each known site seemed to use a different set of fingers, no general consensus could be written.

timeline.finding: CTCF is identified as the protein required for enhancer blocking by HS4 and other vertebrate insulators; in 2000 two groups showed that CTCF binding at the H19 imprinting control region is abolished by CpG methylation, so the methylated paternal allele loses the boundary and expresses Igf2.
timeline.methods: Enhancer-blocking reporter assays, binding-site mutagenesis, in vitro methylation-sensitive binding, transgenic mice
timeline.open: How a single DNA-bound protein blocks an enhancer acting from a distance was unexplained.

timeline.finding: The first genome-wide map finds 13,804 CTCF sites in human fibroblasts, mostly far from transcription start sites, fitting a conserved consensus motif, with occupancy largely invariant across cell types.
timeline.open: Why a minority of sites vary between cell types, and why most genomic matches are unbound, was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Kilobase-resolution Hi-C shows that chromatin loop anchors are usually CTCF-bound and that the two anchoring motifs are overwhelmingly in convergent orientation.
timeline.methods: In situ Hi-C, ChIP-seq, motif-orientation analysis
timeline.open: Whether orientation was causal, and what mechanism could read the orientation of two sites hundreds of kilobases apart, was unknown.

timeline.finding: Deleting or inverting single CTCF sites by CRISPR rewires loops (Sox2, protocadherin and beta-globin loci), showing that orientation is causal; the loop-extrusion model, in which cohesin extrudes DNA until it meets a CTCF site pointing toward it, explains why only convergent pairs form loops.
timeline.methods: CRISPR deletion and inversion with 4C-seq and Hi-C; polymer simulation
timeline.open: Cohesin had not yet been shown to extrude DNA, and how a bound CTCF stops it in one direction only was unknown.

timeline.finding: Two crystal structures of the CTCF finger array on DNA show ZF3-7 each reading three bases of the 15-bp core and explain methylation sensitivity at core position 2 but not 12; on protocadherin sites ZF9-11 read an upstream module, with ZF8 as a spacer.
timeline.open: The two structures disagree about the C-terminal fingers: one places ZF9-11 in the major groove reading module 1, the other finds ZF8-9 spanning the backbone without base contacts and ZF10-11 not visible.

timeline.finding: A 2.7 A structure shows a segment of the CTCF N terminus docking onto the SA2-SCC1 subunits of cohesin, an interaction required specifically for CTCF-anchored loops. Single-molecule imaging in 2023 then showed CTCF blocks extruding cohesin asymmetrically but in a DNA-tension-dependent way, and can redirect extrusion or shrink loops: a regulator of extrusion, not the simple wall the 2015 model assumed.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, Hi-C of interface mutants; in vitro single-molecule imaging of CTCF and cohesin
timeline.open: How permeable CTCF boundaries are to cohesin in living cells, and what sets DNA tension there, was not measured.

open: What CTCF's C-terminal fingers contribute to recognition is unsettled: the protocadherin-site structures place ZF9-11 in the major groove reading the upstream module, whereas the other crystal structure finds ZF8-9 spanning the backbone without base contacts and ZF10-11 disordered, and genome-wide mutant data assign ZF8-11 to non-conserved flanks.

Why most genomic matches to the CTCF core are unbound in a given cell type is only partly explained: CpG methylation at core position 2 accounts for about 41% of variable occupancy across 19 cell types, and the contribution of chromatin accessibility, flanking sequence and cofactors to the remainder has not been quantified.

Whether CTCF acts in cells as a near-absolute barrier to loop extrusion, as the convergent-orientation rule suggests, or as a leaky, tension-dependent one, as single-molecule assays show, is not resolved, because the rate at which cohesin passes CTCF sites in vivo has not been measured.

How much gene regulation depends on CTCF-anchored loops in general is open: acute CTCF degradation dissolves loops and TAD insulation genome-wide, while the clearest transcriptional consequences come from disrupting individual boundaries such as the PDGFRA boundary in IDH-mutant glioma, and which boundaries matter for expression cannot yet be predicted.
